title: Piano Concerto No. 3 in D minor
hook: It begins with a melody that, Rachmaninoff said, wrote itself, and grows into one of the hardest concertos ever written.

painting.title: Blue Morning
painting.pairingNote: New York in 1909, painted by a young American realist in the year Rachmaninoff crossed the Atlantic to give this concerto its first performance there.

facts: Rachmaninoff wrote the concerto in the summer of 1909 and finished it on 23 September, just before his first tour of the United States. He wrote it for that tour, and had so little time that he practised it on a silent keyboard during the voyage.

He played the first performance himself in New York on 28 November 1909, with the New York Symphony Society conducted by Walter Damrosch. Two months later he played it again with Gustav Mahler conducting, and he remembered how Mahler rehearsed every detail long past the scheduled hour.
It is dedicated to the pianist Josef Hofmann, who never played it in public. Rachmaninoff himself preferred it to his Second Concerto, which he found “uncomfortable to play”.

It has a reputation as one of the hardest piano concertos. Vladimir Horowitz, who played it for Rachmaninoff in 1927, made it famous with his recording of 1930. The 1996 film *Shine* made it famous again.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a simple melody grows into a vast first movement with a huge solo [[cadenza|cadenza]] (I), a brooding set of variations (II), a driving finale that brings back the first movement’s themes and ends in triumph in D major (III).

movements.heading: Allegro ma non tanto
movements.summary: After two bars of quiet pulsing in the orchestra, the piano plays a long, plain melody in bare octaves. Everything grows from it. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], but its centre of gravity is the long solo cadenza, which builds to a thunderous climax and then turns quiet as four wind players recall the opening theme.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a simple, narrow melody, like a chant, played by the piano with both hands an octave apart.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a gentler, more yearning melody, introduced by quiet exchanges between orchestra and piano.

stops.hear: A soft, pulsing beat in the orchestra; the piano enters with a plain, quiet melody in octaves
The orchestra takes the melody; the piano weaves fast, busy figures around it
The piano speeds up and becomes restless
Short, quiet exchanges: crisp chords in the orchestra, light replies from the piano
The piano sings a warm, longing melody, freer in tempo
Quietly, the piano recalls the opening melody
Quick, pounding notes in the piano, hands overlapping; the music gets louder and darker, with heavy chords
The orchestra stops; the piano alone builds a long solo to a thunderous climax
Flute, oboe, clarinet and horn each play the opening melody softly, while the piano ripples
The piano alone, very softly, dreams on the second theme
The piano plays the opening melody again, with the orchestra

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: A quiet, rippling close, then a few quick notes

notice: Sing the opening melody to yourself. It moves by small steps and stays in a narrow range, like a chant. Listen for it in all three movements.
In the cadenza’s quiet second part, count the four wind soloists: flute, oboe, clarinet, horn.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Ashkenazy recorded all four Rachmaninoff concertos with Previn and the London Symphony Orchestra for Decca; this Third was recorded in March 1971 and first issued in 1972. Rachmaninoff wrote two versions of the first-movement cadenza; pianists choose one or the other. On the Spotify album the Third is tracks 7–9.

movements.heading: Intermezzo: Adagio
movements.summary: A slow movement built as a set of [[variation|variation]]s on a sad, Russian-sounding tune. The orchestra plays the tune and the first two variations alone before the piano enters. In the middle, a quick, waltz-like episode brings back the first movement’s opening melody. The movement does not end: the piano bursts out and leads straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a long, sorrowful melody, first on the oboe over the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The waltz episode
mainIdeas.description: quick and light, with the first movement’s melody in the woodwinds.

stops.hear: The strings play softly; an oboe sings a long, sad melody
The full strings take the melody, richer and louder
The piano enters with a sudden outburst, then plays its own version of the tune
The piano spreads the tune into rich chords; the music swells to a passionate climax
Lighter and quicker: a waltz-like lilt, with the first movement’s opening melody in clarinet and bassoon while the piano sparkles
stops.happening: The waltz episode, with the theme from movement I

stops.hear: A broad, romantic climax for piano and orchestra
The orchestra returns to the sad opening melody

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The piano breaks in with a violent burst of chords and runs, and goes straight on

notice: Listen for how long the piano waits before entering. The orchestra has the first two minutes to itself.
In the waltz episode, see if you can recognise the first movement’s melody in the woodwinds.

movements.heading: Finale: Alla breve
movements.summary: The finale bursts in without a break. A driving, rhythmic theme in the piano alternates with a broader one in heavy chords. Instead of a normal development there is a long, playful detour, and the first movement’s themes return. Then the main themes come back, the piano builds a dazzling climax, and the second theme bursts out in D major.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: hard-driving and rhythmic, in the piano’s chords.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: broader, a rising tune in heavy chords that becomes the final hymn.

stops.hear: Fast, hammering chords and a driving rhythm in the piano
Bold chords in the piano; a broader tune that rises through heavy, swinging chords
A long, lighter detour: playful, quick and full of new ideas, mostly quiet
stops.happening: The middle section, in E-flat major

stops.hear: Slower and dreamier: the first movement’s two themes come back
The hammering rhythm of the finale’s opening again
The broad tune in heavy chords again
The piano races up and down in a long, glittering build-up, with the orchestra driving it on
The whole orchestra plays the broad tune, slow and grand, in D major; the piano crashes out chords
stops.happening: Theme 2 as a hymn of triumph

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A rush of chords and a final four-note rhythm
stops.happening: The ending; the same short rhythm ends his Second Concerto

notice: Listen for the four-note rhythm at the very end, “dum, da-da, dum”. Rachmaninoff ends his Second Concerto and Second Symphony the same way.
The concerto began in D minor with a plain, quiet melody. It ends in D major with everyone at full volume.

threads.title: One melody
threads.body: The quiet opening tune returns in the second movement’s waltz and in the finale. The concerto is built like a [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]].

threads.title: A Russian sound
threads.body: The opening melody moves like a church chant. One scholar, Joseph Yasser, traced it to a liturgical model; Rachmaninoff said it simply wrote itself.

threads.title: Cuts
threads.body: Rachmaninoff allowed cuts, especially in the second and third movements, and for decades most pianists took them. Today the concerto is usually played complete.

threads.title: Piano first
threads.body: Unlike the Second Concerto, where piano and orchestra are partners, here the piano is the main attraction.
